nameStory: The short-billed dowitcher gets its name from its long, straight bill that's supposedly shorter than its close cousin, the long-billed dowitcher. Ironically, this name is quite misleading since there's so much overlap in bill lengths between the two species that you usually can't tell them apart by bill size alone! The name "dowitcher" itself comes from the Iroquois word "deutsch-er," referring to these probing shorebirds.
description: The short-billed dowitcher is a chunky, medium-sized shorebird with a long, straight bill that looks like a knitting needle. These stocky birds are built for probing deep into mud and sand, with legs positioned well back on their body giving them a distinctive upright posture. They're about the size of a robin but much more robust, with mottled brown and gray plumage that helps them blend into mudflats and shorelines. During breeding season, they develop rusty-orange underparts that make them quite striking against the muddy backgrounds they love.

idTips.label: Sewing machine feeding
idTips.description: Watch for the distinctive rapid-fire probing behavior - they jab their bills up and down into mud so fast it looks like a sewing machine needle, often keeping their heads down while feeding in a rhythmic, mechanical motion

idTips.label: Chunky build
idTips.description: Notice the stocky, robust body shape that's noticeably thicker and more compact than most other sandpipers, with a relatively short neck that gives them a hunched appearance

idTips.label: Straight, dark bill
idTips.description: Look for the long, perfectly straight bill that's dark colored and appears slightly swollen at the tip when viewed up close, quite different from curved bills of other shorebirds

idTips.label: Greenish-yellow legs
idTips.description: Check for the distinctive greenish-yellow to olive-colored legs that stand out against dark mud - they're never bright yellow or orange like some similar species

idTips.label: White rump patch
idTips.description: When they fly, watch for the bright white wedge extending up the back from the rump, creating a distinctive white triangle that's easily visible against their darker wings and back

idTips.label: Group feeding behavior
idTips.description: Often seen feeding in tight flocks where multiple birds probe the same productive muddy area, creating a soft chorus of squelching sounds as bills penetrate wet sediment

habitat: Look for short-billed dowitchers along New England's coastal mudflats, salt marshes, and shallow tidal pools where soft sediment allows easy probing. They're commonly found in places like Plum Island in Massachusetts or the Connecticut River estuary, favoring areas where fresh water meets salt water. During migration, they also visit inland locations like muddy pond edges, flooded fields, and sewage treatment ponds where the substrate is soft enough for their feeding style.

seasonality.spring: Peak migration occurs from late April through May, when birds show a mix of breeding and non-breeding plumages. This is an excellent time to see them as they're actively feeding to fuel their journey north to Arctic breeding grounds.
seasonality.summer: Few birds remain in New England during summer, with most having departed for northern breeding territories. Any dowitchers seen in summer are likely non-breeding individuals or early fall migrants.
seasonality.fall: Migration extends from July through October, with peak numbers in August and September. Birds show more variation in plumage, including juveniles with fresh, crisp feather patterns and adults in various stages of molt.
seasonality.winter: Generally absent from New England during winter months, as these birds migrate to warmer coastal areas from the mid-Atlantic south to South America. Any winter sightings would be quite unusual.

funFact: Short-billed dowitchers can actually taste what they're touching underground - they have sensitive nerve endings at their bill tips that let them detect and identify prey buried in mud without even seeing it, essentially "tasting" their way to a meal in complete darkness beneath the surface!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with the long-billed dowitcher, which is nearly identical in appearance. The best way to tell them apart is by voice - short-billed dowitchers give a mellow "tu-tu-tu" call, while long-billed dowitchers make a sharp "keek" sound. Remember: "short-billed = soft call, long-billed = loud call" for the easiest identification trick.
contextualKnowledge: Despite their names, you cannot reliably identify short-billed versus long-billed dowitchers by bill length alone - there's too much overlap between the species. These two species were actually considered the same bird until 1950, and field identification between them remains one of the most challenging puzzles in North American birding even today.
compareHints: Compared to its only close relative, the long-billed dowitcher, the short-billed species typically shows more barring on the flanks during breeding season and has a slightly less bulbous bill tip. However, voice is the most reliable difference - short-billed dowitchers give softer, more musical calls compared to the sharp, single-note calls of long-billed dowitchers. Long-billed dowitchers also tend to prefer freshwater habitats while short-billed favor saltwater coastal areas.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to the short-billed dowitcher, the long-billed has a noticeably longer, thinner bill and prefers freshwater habitats over salt marshes.
